subject: Communication
title: Ad Hominem: Attacking the Person, Not the Point
description: Learn Ad Hominem: Attacking the Person, Not the Point in one minute.

hook.text: 'You can't trust his climate data — he's funded by the government!' Attack the person, dodge the evidence.

buildup.text: Ad hominem attacks the character, motive, or background of the arguer instead of addressing the argument itself.

discovery.text: It's the most common fallacy in political debates. Instead of engaging with policy, opponents question credibility.

twist.text: Sometimes the source does matter. A tobacco-funded study on smoking risks deserves extra scrutiny.

climax.text: The test: would this argument be true if someone else said it? If yes, the person's identity is irrelevant to the logic.

punchline.text: When they attack the person instead of the point, they've run out of points.

quiz.question: What is an ad hominem fallacy?
options: Attacking the person instead of the argument

details.summary: An ad hominem fallacy attacks the person making an argument rather than addressing the argument itself. Dismissing a claim because the speaker is young, biased, or hypocritical does not refute the claim's logic or evidence. It is the most common fallacy in public discourse.
details.whyItMatters: Recognizing ad hominem attacks prevents you from being distracted from the actual argument. It is also the easiest fallacy to accidentally commit.
takeaways: Attack the argument, not the person making it
A flawed messenger does not necessarily mean a flawed message
Ad hominem is the most common fallacy in political debate

faq.question: Is it ever relevant to question the person instead of the argument?
faq.answer: Yes, when credibility is genuinely at issue. If someone claims expertise they do not have, questioning their qualifications is legitimate. But this challenges their ethos, not their argument. The argument itself must still be evaluated on its own logical merits.

faq.question: What is the difference between ad hominem and a valid character critique?
faq.answer: Ad hominem replaces argument evaluation with personal attack. A valid character critique adds context to an argument without dismissing it. Saying this person lied before, so their data might need extra scrutiny is fair. Saying they lied before, so they are wrong is fallacious.
